item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Well, it’s been a while since I last made a post. A lot of things have happened and changed in tech, and in my life. I got a good job on a good team working with Go, I got to go to Japan for a little over two weeks (something I’ve wanted to do since I was about eight years old), I’ve read a lot of books, started working on a side project I’ve had in mind for a while now, got heavily into Balatro (which re-inspired me to start making games again — something I’ve always wanted to do and have only done once before on a very small scale). I also got into sandbag lifting (so dang fun), started skateboarding more, and I’m not far off from getting my Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu purple belt. So yeah, it’s been a cool year — but that’s not all that happened.

During mid-summer my wife was laid off shortly after being told she wouldn’t be. That really sucked, but she took it like a champion and has since started her own web design business. Regardless, it was not a fair situation after she’d been told she was doing a great job and was part of the core team — one of those “it’s not you, it’s us” scenarios. Fast-forward a few months and I’m writing this roughly seven weeks after getting laid off myself. I was also blindsided. Not cool, but I’ll save the details for another time.

What’s the point?

I’m mostly writing all of this to reflect, vent, and plant a flag in the digital ground that I can look back on a year from now. I’ve been getting paid to make things on computers since 2018. It started with maps and some automation, which led to a career pivot into “coding” (I thought frontend/websites), but I’ve mostly only ever been in backend-heavy software engineering roles for the last six years. Over that time I’ve worked at four places — all the way from red-tape hell with 500k employees down to a startup with about 100 folks, and a few places in between. I’ve been on seven different teams with seven different managers. I’ve led planning discussions, mentored other devs in my wheelhouse, worked alongside system architects to lay the groundwork for big ideas I spearheaded, been forward-deployed in the feature trenches, worked the firehose, worn the ops hat, and managed my own Docker/Kubernetes configs for microservices I ported out of unscalable implementations. I’ve done a lot, worked with a lot of people, and seen a crap-ton of management styles, scenarios, bad ideas, failures, successes, good ideas, and everything in between.

Yet here I am. No W-2, and to be honest, a little burned out in the age of AI — arguably one of the weirdest times in tech in the last twenty years. Very much a “damned if you use it, damned if you don’t” moment, at least from my perspective. The old heads (not all of them) tend to be skeptical and really don’t like anyone under them using it. There’s no agreed-upon “here’s how we use it” policy across the industry, yet all the CEOs love it and can’t help but see dollar signs in savings and sales. It’s quite the dilemma and pretty dang toxic if you ask me. Tech is weird at the moment, and I don’t see it changing anytime soon.

Having seen and done so much, I can’t help but think this isn’t worth it. This constant uphill grind only to be tossed aside unfairly, all while being told “dance, monkey, dance,” with very little support. Is it worth it? Outsourcing, underpaying, belittling, blaming, poor communication, constant churn, ego, tech-bro attitudes — none of this sounds good, right? If I described the software running your next flight with any of those adjectives, you probably wouldn’t want to get on that plane. So why is it that, of all the places I’ve worked and people I’ve worked with, I can count on maybe two hands the folks who genuinely cared about doing a good job, helping others, and seeing teams, teammates, and the company grow and win? Not just good people — amazing people. Y’all know who you are.

What is the point? A paycheck? Frustration? Comfort? Products? A W-2? I’m not sure. We all have to pay our bills and most of us want to do a good job at the end of the day. But given all the crazy, I can’t help but think there’s a better way. I’m not a perfect person or a perfect engineer, but I do care about people, I do see what I do as a craft, and I personally want what I build to be right and fast. That said, I’m unwilling to be a jerk or throw others under the bus just to save my own skin. I never wanted to be a 10× engineer, and I don’t really care to define myself solely as a programmer. I just like having a craft, tinkering, polishing, and doing a good job.

Where are we at and where are we going?

So where does that leave me? Where does that leave other engineers like me? To be honest, I’m not sure. At the moment, I’m working for myself — coding, consulting, and a few other things. Big Tech is big annoying right now, and I just want to build things unhindered for a while.

So I guess to some degree I’m taking a career break (can we still call it that???). I’m going solo for a bit, and honestly, I wouldn’t be surprised if a lot more devs end up doing the same in the coming years. As a dev with six years of real experience I have a ton of skills now. Sure, there’s still plenty I don’t know and haven’t built. Yeah, I couldn’t just hop into Google and hit the ground running (news flash — most folks can’t), but that doesn’t matter for most businesses. Most companies don’t need to operate like Google; most just need a little software and a little automation, not full-time devs forever. Honestly, in the years to come I think the need for a competent dev to come in, help out for a while, and then check in periodically will only grow. That’s where I plan to spend my skills for the time being.

AI is only going to even the skill gap further for everyone. I think devs should take time to think about that and what they actually want to do with their lives and skills. To be honest, coding is a means to an end. Sure — tinker, build, make that game, work your gig, etc. — but take it as a lesson from me rambling here: your W-2 isn’t safe. You are a valued employee until you’re not. Don’t count on getting comfortable in your job or your skills. Get comfortable being uncomfortable and have fun with it.

That’s it. Rant done.

I’ll be doing more writing here about solo web dev and solo game dev in the future.

item.content:encoded:
From Geology & Naval Warfare Maps to Go Developer

Hi, I’m Cole. My programming journey began in late 2019, but my path there was anything but direct. After studying Geology in college and working as a Field Geologist for about a year, I found myself creating maps for naval warfare ships at the US DOD. It was there that I first dipped my toes into bash scripting to automate my workflow, and I was instantly hooked.

When 2020 rolled around, like many others with extra time on their hands, I dove deeper into programming. What fascinated me most was the democratization of the field - anyone willing to put in the time and effort could become a programmer, regardless of their background. This realization was particularly exciting for someone like me, coming from a non-traditional tech background. I started with basic C programming, creating simple programs like “Hello World” and a basic calculator. Initially, I thought I wanted to be a ‘frontend developer’, so I also dabbled in HTML and CSS. Little did I know that this curiosity would lead me on a path of learning Javascript, React, .Net/C#, SQL, Java/Springboot, TypeScript, Python, Go and a bit more.

A turning point came when I read an article about a former geologist who transitioned into programming. I reached out to him (thanks, Adam!) and our chat about geology, programming, and the tech lifestyle convinced me to take the plunge. I quit my job and committed to becoming a work-from-home dev. The challenge of programming, the flexibility of remote work, and the potential earnings were too tempting to resist. I moved back home and enrolled in a course with Tech901, where I learned the basics of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Shortly after, Cook Systems reached out and put me through an intensive bootcamp focused on Java and Spring Boot. I’m super grateful to both of these organizations as they paved the way for the path I’m on today. After going through Cook’s fast paced bootcamp, almost immediately, I landed a job as a Backend Developer (not frontend, ironically) at FedEx through Cook. Despite feeling underprepared as do most early career devs, I embraced the challenge and learned rapidly. After a year, I felt I had truly cut my teeth in programming professionally, then my career took another turn.

A company called Green Mountain (formerly Green Mountain Technology) ‘GM’ contacted me about a frontend position. Although I ended up in a backend role with C#/.NET on team Honey Badgers (a whole blog post of its self, super talented devs), my time at GM was transformative. I learned about software engineering, unit testing, performance optimization, SQL, Kafka, APIs, architecture, code reviews, mentoring/how to mentor others, and project ownership. The experience and mentorship I received at GM were invaluable, its what helped my find my love for backend programming. However, like many tech companies in 2022-2023, GM faced layoffs. After about two years with GM, I decided it was time to spread my wings further. This led me to Hone Health, a fast-paced telehealth startup where I’ve been for about a year. At Hone, I’ve worn many hats - from helpdesk to bug hunting, infrastructure work to feature development, you name it and I’ve done it. As I write this, I’m transitioning to a new role as a Go developer - an exciting new chapter in my career. This journey thus far has been filled with challenges, growth, and unexpected turns. I’m looking forward to sharing more about my ongoing learning and experiences in future blog posts. Expect lots of post about Go.

~ Stay tuned as I continue to document my adventures in software development, and hopefully improve my writing along the way! 😆
